prompts.question: Evaluate Bongiorno’s interpretation of the aims and purposes of history. Use Source A and at least TWO other sources to support your argument.
markerNotes: The strongest answers first state what Bongiorno's interpretation claims (history's public purpose, and the duty of rigour that follows from its misuse) and then test that claim. They evaluate the interpretation rather than summarising Source A.

Source A and the other sources must do argumentative work. Each source is placed beside a claim and either supports it, qualifies it or complicates it, so the response integrates them rather than listing them.
Evaluation needs a standard of judgement. A top answer asks what Bongiorno counts as legitimate use of history and whether rigour can supply the standard that his critique assumes.
Historiographical awareness shows in naming the live debates (objectivity, presentism, relativism) and in explaining what each debate means for Bongiorno's position, not in a list of names.

Accepts Bongiorno's account of history's misuse without testing whether his examples show what he claims about the aims of history rather than about its abuse.
Confuses the aims of history with the uses made of it, so the answer discusses who benefited from history rather than what the discipline is for.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Frank Bongiorno's interpretation of the aims and purposes of history in Source A is that these cannot be separated from its public responsibilities. He begins with the attractions of studying one's own place and group, then argues that the discipline has often served the powerful. Its assumptions, methodologies and temporalities, he argues, have helped justify colonialism, war, genocide and environmental destruction. From this he draws two purposes. Historians must be trained with the rigour expected of professions such as medicine or engineering, and they must contribute to the public life of a democracy in an era of myth and contempt for expertise. I argue that Bongiorno identifies the stakes of historical work convincingly, but that he treats the discipline's civic function as more settled than historiography allows, and that his remedy of rigour depends on a standard of judgement that is itself contested.

The strongest part of Source A is its account of misuse, which historians have long had to confront. Edward Said's Orientalism (1978) showed how Western scholarship produced a body of knowledge about the East that supported imperial rule. In Australia, Henry Reynolds's The Other Side of the Frontier (1981) argued that much national history had neglected frontier violence and Aboriginal resistance. The legal consequences of a historical assumption became visible in Mabo v Queensland (No 2) (1992), when the High Court rejected the doctrine of terra nullius, the idea that Australia belonged to no one when British settlement began in 1788. The temporalities that Bongiorno mentions have a similar history. The habit of placing some societies at an earlier stage of development cast them as less advanced, a judgement that colonial rule could then claim to correct. Bongiorno is right that historical claims can be mobilised to justify dispossession, and that historians answer for what their work is used to prove.

Bongiorno's account of purpose is less secure when history is treated as a public good to be defended. E. H. Carr, in What Is History? (1961), argued that the facts a historian selects are shaped by the questions of the present, so that history is an ongoing exchange between the historian and the past. Carr's account supports Bongiorno's view that history is never politically innocent, but it complicates his distinction between legitimate and illegitimate uses. If every historical account reflects present concerns, a critique of misuse needs a standard against which uses can be judged. Source A assumes that rigour supplies that standard. The question is whether a discipline whose questions are always partly political can supply it.

Richard Evans, in In Defence of History (1997), gives that standard a firmer footing. Against postmodern relativism, he argues that the past can be known imperfectly but genuinely, because evidence can be tested and some interpretations are better supported than others. On this view Bongiorno's demand for rigour is not a retreat to older objectivity but a defence of the procedures that separate myth from evidence. Evans's argument strengthens Source A, but it also locates history's public value in its method rather than in its civic role. Source A does not explain how the public life Bongiorno wants can be kept free of the partisan uses it condemns.

The interpretation and perspective of Source A have a weakness of their own. Source A gives the study of one's own place a warning, yet the histories written to recover the voices of excluded groups, including Reynolds's, are the very work that serves Bongiorno's public purpose. Nor is the post-truth framing self-evident: misinformation about the past existed long before the present era, and the historian's authority has always rested on method more than on public trust. Bongiorno's interpretation is therefore most convincing as a call to hold historians to professional standards, and least convincing as a complete account of history's aims. Historians pursue several purposes: to establish what happened, to explain why it happened, and to contribute to public judgement. Bongiorno rightly insists that the third matters, but the first two are the foundation on which it stands.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 21-25 row. It evaluates Bongiorno's interpretation rather than describing it, integrates Source A with Carr, Evans, Said, Reynolds and the Mabo decision, and reaches a qualified judgement that his remedy of rigour rests on a contested standard. No case study is needed for this question.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Bongiorno's interpretation in Source A is that history has a public purpose and that historians must take responsibility for how their work is used. He argues that history has often served the powerful, and that its assumptions have supported colonialism, war and environmental destruction. He also argues that historians should be trained to a high standard and should take part in public debate, because this is needed to counter myth and the rejection of expertise. The interpretation is important and can be tested against other historians.

The point about misuse is supported by evidence. Reynolds's The Other Side of the Frontier shows that Australian histories often ignored frontier violence, so history helped make dispossession seem acceptable. The High Court's decision in Mabo in 1992 also showed how the idea of terra nullius had been used to justify taking Aboriginal land, and the court rejected it. These examples show that Bongiorno is right that history can be used to justify wrong actions.

Carr's What Is History? suggests that historians always select facts based on their own concerns, so all history is affected by the present. This makes it harder to say which uses of history are misuses. Bongiorno seems to think rigour can solve this problem, but it is not clear that it can.

Evans's In Defence of History argues that the past can be known through evidence and that some interpretations are better than others. This supports Bongiorno's call for rigour, because historians can test claims and public history can be more accurate. Bongiorno's argument is therefore fairly convincing, although it could be more balanced. Evans's approach would also help a reader decide whether a public use of history is honest, because a museum display, a documentary or a textbook can be checked against the same evidence as a scholarly book.

Overall, the interpretation is persuasive because it identifies the dangers of history and asks historians to act responsibly. It is less convincing when it treats the civic role of history as its most important purpose, because historians also seek to understand the past accurately.

To lift it, test a claim against a named source and say what that evidence shows about Bongiorno's case.

sampleAnswers.answer: Bongiorno says history has a public purpose. He thinks history has been used by powerful people to support things like colonialism and war, so historians need to be careful about what they write. He also says historians should be trained properly and should take part in public debate. Reynolds's book is an example of a historian who wrote about the frontier in Australia, and it shows that history can be important. Overall, Bongiorno's view seems reasonable, and historians should think about how their work is used by others. This matters because people use history to make decisions about land, rights and the past.

prompts.question: Evaluate the role of historians in changing interpretations and perspectives of history. Integrate Sources A and B and at least TWO other sources throughout your response.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Historians change interpretations of the past by making narrative and argument public, so that others can test and contest them. Tom Holt and Rita Luís and Chrysi Rapanta describe this role in different terms. Holt, in Thinking Historically (1990), treats the historian as a narrator who builds a plot from documents, and wants students to learn the questions that turn documents into a story. Luís and Rapanta argue that disciplinary history is an ongoing debate in which historians convince audiences through evidence, rebuttal and counterclaim. Evaluating the role of historians means asking what they change, and whether their work alters the aims and purposes of history or only the interpretations within it. I argue that historians change interpretations considerably, mainly by changing the questions asked of the past, rather than by revealing a single truth.

Holt’s Source A is most persuasive where it shows that historians do not simply report evidence. He writes that history is ‘fundamentally and inescapably narrative’, and that historians work with plots, imposing order on past experience. This matters for interpretation because a plot decides which events are significant. An interpretation changes when a historian gives a different plot to the same documents. Carr’s What Is History? (1961) made a similar point: the historian selects and interprets facts, so interpretations change as historians change their questions. Holt’s advice that students ask whether a document is primary or secondary, what it leaves out and what it assumes shows the same process at school level. Historians change interpretations by changing which documents seem significant and what they seem to say.

Luís and Rapanta, in their review of historical reasoning competence, offer a second account of the historian’s role. Historians present evidence-based interpretations and convince an audience ‘via verbal argument’. New interpretations come from new sources or new readings, and a historian must be able to rebut counterclaims. For a historical interpretation to stand, it must survive contest. This account treats historical work as argumentation rather than the discovery of a fixed story, and it explains why historians matter: they keep argument alive. Yet it also limits the claim that historians change interpretations alone. The new theories and sources they draw on come from outside the discipline, and an argument is accepted only if the audience finds it plausible.

The difference between interpretations and perspectives matters for evaluation. An interpretation is a claim about what happened and why. A perspective is the standpoint from which the past is seen. Historians change interpretations by revising claims about evidence, and they change perspectives by bringing new questions about who the past is for. G.R. Elton’s The Practice of History (1967) held that the discipline lies in the rigorous testing of evidence, so historians change interpretations through disciplined method. Changes in perspective often come from outside the profession: from social movements, from new audiences, and from historians of women and labour who asked questions the older narratives had not. The historian’s role is therefore to translate outside change into argument that can be tested.

Judged against these accounts, the historian’s role is decisive for interpretations and less decisive for perspectives. Holt shows that a historian’s plot can change what a document seems to mean, and Luís and Rapanta show that plausibility is decided in public argument. Their weakness is that both describe the process in general terms. Natalie Zemon Davis’s The Return of Martin Guerre (1983) offers a case. By reconstructing a sixteenth-century court case from the French countryside, she showed how a historian’s narrative can make readers reconsider the motives of the people involved, including the wife who lived with the impostor. Her work changed the interpretation of a single case, and through it the question historians asked about individual motives.

The historiography of the last century shows the limits of the historian’s role as well. A historian cannot change an interpretation that no one reads. The audience decides whether a narrative is plausible, and that audience is shaped by schools, media and public memory. Holt’s advice to students suggests that influence begins in the classroom, while Luís and Rapanta imply that it depends on rebuttal and peer review. Historians change interpretations through a shared discipline rather than as isolated individuals. The process makes change reliable, but it also means the most significant changes often come from shifts in what the audience asks.

Historians have a major role in changing interpretations and perspectives of history, but the role is best understood as making arguments that others can test. Holt shows how narrative and selection change what a document means. Luís and Rapanta show how argument decides what survives contest. Carr, Elton and Davis show that this process can change interpretations of individual cases and of the discipline itself. Historians change perspectives less directly, because perspective comes from the questions the audience brings. The role is real, and it is most powerful where the historian makes the change of perspective explicit and open to rebuttal.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 21–25 row: it makes an insightful judgement on the historian’s role, integrates Sources A and B by setting them against each other, and uses Carr, Elton and Davis to show the change in interpretation and perspective.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Historians play a large part in changing interpretations and perspectives of history. Sources A and B both describe the historian’s work, though in different ways. Tom Holt’s Source A says history is narrative and that students should learn to question documents. Rita Luís and Chrysi Rapanta’s Source B says history is a debate, in which historians present evidence-based interpretations and convince an audience through argument.

Holt’s point is that narrative and plot shape what historians say. He says historians work with plots and that a narrative imposes order on past experience. A historian who uses the same documents can therefore produce a different interpretation by choosing a different plot. Holt also says historians ask whether a source is primary or secondary and what it leaves out, which suggests that historians change interpretations by asking new questions of familiar sources.

Luís and Rapanta argue that historians persuade audiences, and that new interpretations come from new sources or new readings based on theories. They say an interpretation must be able to rebut counterclaims. This suggests the role of historians is to take part in argument, so interpretation changes through a process of challenge.

E.H. Carr’s What Is History? also supports the view that historians change interpretations because they select facts. G.R. Elton’s The Practice of History argued that historians should work through sources with discipline. These two books show that the historian’s role is central to how history is understood, but they also suggest that the historian works within a wider community.

Historians change perspectives as well as interpretations, though perspectives are influenced by society. Overall, the historian has an important role in changing interpretations and perspectives of history, but this role depends on the wider debate and on the audience. The evaluation is therefore that the role is significant but not solitary. Holt’s stress on the questions a historian asks of a source is a clear case of change without new evidence, because the same document can be read for a new purpose. The evaluation would be stronger with one clear example of a historian changing an interpretation, but the two sources describe the process rather than a case.

Source B says historians argue with each other and use evidence. These sources show that historians do things like making arguments and finding sources. Historians change how people see the past. History is different now from what it was before because of historians and their work. Historians are a major part of the subject, so they change interpretations quite a lot, and this is interesting to study. Their work matters for the way the past is understood.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Historians can be certain about a great deal, but not about everything, and the distinction matters. Katie Engelhart presents historians as witnesses in courtrooms, where their claims are tested by lawyers who want guilt or innocence, and where historians are accused of speculating. Richard J Evans writes about a libel trial in which historians gave expert evidence against David Irving's claims, and he argues that the trial showed the reasoned conclusions historians can reach. This response argues that historians can be certain about particular claims that rest on verifiable evidence, but that certainty about the larger meaning of the past is limited. The question is therefore one of degree, and the degree depends on the kind of claim being made.

Engelhart describes a past 'dragged reluctantly' before judges and juries, in which historians 'opine and speculate' while witnesses must swear an oath that their testimony is the truth. Her core question is whether historians can be certain enough about anything to swear an oath on it. The problem she identifies is real. Historical conclusions are probabilistic, revisable and framed by argument, while a court needs a verdict. Her source therefore shows a gap between the historian's form of certainty and the law's. Its scepticism is aimed at the certainty the courtroom demands, which is not the form historians usually produce.

Evans offers a counter-claim grounded in the trial itself. He argues that the trial showed the ability of historians to reach reasoned and persuasive conclusions on the basis of a fair-minded examination of the evidence. Its significance was that attempts to discredit the evidence 'rested on demonstrable forgery and falsification'. Certainty here does not mean that every detail of the past is secured. It means that some claims can be shown false, and that the charge of forgery can itself be tested and disproved. Evans's argument also rests on a logical point: if there is such a thing as historical untruth, there must be historical truth against which it is measured.

Evans's certainty is limited, however. He admits that the evidence was not 'totally flawless', and that concession matters because it separates two kinds of certainty. A historian can be certain that a document is forged when the forgery can be demonstrated, or that a date is wrong when a register contradicts it. A historian is much less certain about motive, intention or the meaning of a process, where the evidence allows more than one reading and where Engelhart's expert witnesses must offer an argument rather than a fact. The objectivity Evans defends is therefore the objectivity of method, not of conclusion.

Keith Jenkins's Re-thinking History (1991) supplies the sceptical position against which Evans's claim should be tested. Jenkins argues that history is a discourse, a way of writing shaped by the historian's position and language, and that the past can be reached only through texts. On this view certainty is the certainty of a narrative within a discourse, and disagreement about the same evidence shows the limits of any claim to truth. Jenkins is right that historians select and frame their evidence, as Carr also argued, but his position struggles to explain how a forgery can be identified at all. Evans's example requires a standard outside the discourse, and the trial shows historians using one, which is the point at which relativism must answer to evidence.

The judgement therefore depends on what kind of claim is in question. Where a claim can be checked against independent records, as the forgery in the trial could be, historians can be certain to a high degree, and Engelhart's courtroom standard is largely met. Where a claim concerns the meaning of events or the intentions of actors, certainty is probable at best. Engelhart's historians 'opine and speculate' in that second category, and her critics are right that a courtroom is a poor setting for such argument. Yet the historian's task is not to achieve the courtroom's certainty. It is to show how strongly the evidence supports each conclusion, and to say where the argument goes beyond it.

Historians can be certain to a considerable extent about particular, testable claims, and Evans's trial shows that certainty is attainable where forgery and falsification can be demonstrated. They cannot be certain about the larger meaning of the past, which depends on argument, selection and judgement. Engelhart is right that the courtroom asks a different question, and Jenkins is right that historical narratives are constructed. Yet the existence of demonstrable falsehood means that certainty is not an illusion, and that historical evidence can settle some questions beyond dispute. The most accurate answer is that historians can be certain of what the evidence establishes, and must be candid about how far an interpretation goes beyond it. The historiography of such trials records how far that candour has been practised.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: it gives a sustained judgement that certainty depends on the kind of claim, and it integrates Engelhart, Evans and Jenkins, with Evans's concession used as evidence. The conclusion weighs the sources against each other rather than restating them.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Historians can be certain about some things, but the trial that Evans describes shows that certainty has limits. Engelhart's article presents a courtroom in which historians are expert witnesses and critics say that historians 'opine and speculate'. Her question is whether historians can be certain enough about anything to swear an oath on it. This is a useful test, although it asks for a form of certainty historians rarely claim for their work, and the critics may be setting the standard too high.

Evans responds that the trial showed historians reaching reasoned and persuasive conclusions from the evidence. He argues that attempts to discredit the evidence rested on demonstrable forgery and falsification. This is a real example of certainty, because a forgery can be shown to be a forgery. Evans also admits that the evidence was not totally flawless, so his certainty is not total, and that admission is an important part of his argument.

Keith Jenkins's Re-thinking History (1991) offers a more sceptical view. Jenkins argues that history is a discourse shaped by language and the historian's position, so that a historian's certainty is the certainty of a narrative. This challenges Evans, because the identification of a forgery seems to require a standard outside the narrative. The sceptical view explains why historians disagree about the same evidence, but it does not explain how a forgery can be found in the first place. A student who takes both positions seriously can see that the trial sits between them.

Overall, historians can be certain to a considerable extent about specific claims that rest on evidence, such as forgery or the dating of a document. They are much less certain about the meaning of events and the intentions of the people in them. The question is therefore one of degree, and historians should say how far their interpretation goes beyond the evidence they can check. Engelhart's question is useful because it forces that distinction into the open. Evans's example is a good one because it shows a specific claim that can be tested.

Historians therefore need to be careful about what they claim and should say when they are speculating about the past. Each source gives a different answer about how certain the past can be.

sampleAnswers.answer:
My case study is the frontier in Australia. The question asks me to evaluate the influence of context on historical interpretation, and I will test that influence on two areas of debate: the extent and character of frontier violence, and the place of Aboriginal perspectives in frontier histories. Source C is a cartoon in which a figure with a speech bubble says 'Don't believe everything you read' while a seated figure draws an elephant on a cave wall. It makes the point that every record has a maker with a purpose, and that the audience must judge it. This response argues that the context of producers of history strongly shapes which questions historians ask and which sources they weigh, but that its influence is limited where documentary evidence can be checked.

Source C is a useful way into the question because it presents a record made by one person, for an audience that may doubt it. The seated figure draws the animal on the wall, and the sceptical figures do not know whether to believe it. The cartoon exposes a basic point: the form and claims of a record depend on who makes it and why. Applied to the frontier, settler diaries, official despatches and court records are the wall drawings. The historian who reads them must ask who wrote them, for whom, and what the writing was meant to justify. Context therefore lies in the producer and in the reader, and both are present whenever a record is used.

Henry Reynolds's The Other Side of the Frontier (1981) shows context at work. Reynolds read settler records against the grain to argue that Aboriginal resistance was a central part of the frontier, and that settler violence was more widespread than earlier histories admitted. The book appeared as the land rights movement was gaining momentum, and a new generation of historians was challenging a national story in which the frontier was a peaceful advance of settlement. The context did not supply the evidence. It set the question: why had the violence been left out, and who had decided that it was not important?

Keith Windschuttle's The Fabrication of Aboriginal History, Volume One (2002) challenged this interpretation, and the context of its publication is central to its significance. Windschuttle argued that estimates of Aboriginal deaths in Van Diemen's Land had been inflated, because historians relied on secondary sources and selected evidence. The book appeared during the history wars, a public dispute in which critics of the account of frontier violence described it as politically motivated. Windschuttle's own selection of records was also contested, which shows that context influences critics as much as the authors they criticise.

The context of the 1990s is also visible in the changing place of Aboriginal perspectives. The High Court's Mabo decision of 1992 recognised native title and changed the legal meaning of land on the frontier. Historians who wrote after it were more likely to treat Aboriginal people as agents with their own purposes, rather than as objects of settler policy. The shift changed the questions. Historians asked how Aboriginal people responded to, adapted to and resisted the frontier, not only how settlers took land. This shift had its own limits, because Aboriginal perspectives in the colonial archive are fragmentary and must often be read through settler documents.

Context does not determine every interpretation, however. Where records of killings, official instructions and police and military reports survive, they constrain what can be argued. Windschuttle's critics and his defenders both had to engage the documents, and the best work on frontier violence has tested claims against sources rather than settling the answer in advance. A historian in the 1980s and one in the 2000s could read the same colonial despatch and agree on what it says, while disagreeing about why it was written or how far its claims should be trusted. Context therefore influences the questions and the weight given to evidence more than it changes the content of the documents.

Context has a strong influence on the historiography of the frontier in Australia. The political climate of the 1980s encouraged historians to place Aboriginal resistance and settler violence at the centre of the story, and the history wars of the 2000s encouraged scepticism about counts and sources. Source C reminds the reader that every record has a maker and an audience, and that historians and their critics are shaped by their own contexts. Yet context does not decide everything. Documents and testimony constrain what can plausibly be claimed, and the debate about frontier violence has advanced where historians tested their claims against the surviving record. The influence of context is therefore profound in the questions historians ask and the weight they give evidence, but limited in the evidence itself. Source criticism, applied to both settler and Aboriginal sources, is the means by which that limit is reached.

The conclusion separates the influence on questions from the limit imposed by the evidence.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The case study is the Anzacs, and the area of debate is whether the Anzac legend records what the soldiers of the First World War experienced, or what later Australians needed to believe about them. The context of producers of history bears directly on this statement. The recording of history is shaped by historians’ individual contexts, and for the Anzacs each major account was written by someone whose position, politics and audience affected what was recorded. I judge the statement largely true, while recognising that the soldiers’ own letters and diaries constrained every historian who used them.

Charles Bean was the official war correspondent of the Australian Imperial Force and later the author of the official history of Australia in the First World War. His The Story of Anzac (1921) gave the national story its enduring shape: the landing at Gallipoli on 25 April 1915 as a test of national character, and the soldier as a figure of mateship and sacrifice. Bean’s context mattered. He wrote in the 1920s, when the nation was building memorials and seeking meaning for its losses, and he was closely involved with the Australian War Memorial. The collection and the narrative he helped to build selected the evidence later historians inherited. The official history recorded the Anzacs, but it recorded them as Bean’s generation wished to remember them.

Bill Gammage’s The Broken Years (1974) changed the record by making soldiers’ own words the main evidence. Drawing on the letters and diaries of about a thousand front-line soldiers, most held in the Australian War Memorial, Gammage showed a war experienced as hardship, grief and endurance, not only as triumph. His context was the 1970s, a period when social history and the study of ordinary people were attracting historians. His questions, about what the war felt like to the men who fought it, were the questions of his moment, and they produced an Anzac different from Bean’s. The soldier in Gammage is less a symbol of national character than a person trying to survive.

Ken Inglis’s Sacred Places: War Memorials in the Australian Landscape (1998) moved the debate from the soldiers to the memorials. Inglis argued that the imagery, ceremonies and rhetoric around war memorials formed a civil religion, a cult of Anzac, that gave the nation a sense of sacred purpose. His context was late-twentieth-century Australia, a national culture in which commemoration was central to public life, and his book treats the memorial as evidence of what the living needed from the dead. The same material can support very different national identity stories, depending on the historian’s questions. Inglis writes the Anzac legend as a national religion, while Gammage writes the soldiers’ war.

Marilyn Lake and Henry Reynolds, in What’s Wrong with Anzac? The Militarisation of Australian History (2010, with Mark McKenna and Joy Damousi), wrote from a different context again: the revival of Anzac Day from the 1990s and heavy government spending on commemoration as the centenary approached. They argued that the legend had come to crowd out other national stories, such as the achievements of democratic reform and the frontier wars, and that it was being used to teach a military version of national identity. Their question, what the Anzac story leaves out and whose interests its prominence serves, produces a different Anzac from the earlier accounts of courage and mateship.

Judged against these accounts, the statement holds to a considerable extent, but not in every respect. Bean, Gammage, Inglis and Lake and Reynolds each show a historian’s context shaping what was recorded, and their disagreements are the area of debate. The evidence is largely shared, however. Bean and Gammage both drew on soldiers’ records, so the disagreement is less about the existence of evidence than about which evidence counts as typical and what the historian takes the war to have been for. A historian’s context selects questions and frames answers, but the record is not infinitely elastic. A soldier’s letter that describes fear cannot be turned into a story of cheerful sacrifice without being misread.

The recording of the Anzacs has been shaped by historians’ individual contexts to a large degree. Bean’s commitment to a national story after 1918, Gammage’s concern with ordinary soldiers in the 1970s, Inglis’s interest in memorial religion and Lake and Reynolds’ critique of the legend’s place in national memory each produced a different Anzac. The statement is therefore largely true, but its limit is that the soldiers’ own letters and diaries constrained every account. Historians are shaped by context, yet the sources keep a voice that context cannot entirely silence.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 21–25 row: it names the case study and the area of debate at the start, gives a judgement that is qualified by the evidence, and integrates four historians whose contexts are explained and compared.

The case study is the Anzacs. The area of debate is whether the Anzac legend shows what soldiers experienced or what Australians wanted to believe. The statement says the recording of history is shaped by historians’ individual contexts. I think this is partly true, although the sources also matter.

Charles Bean wrote the official history of Australia in the First World War. His book The Story of Anzac presented the soldiers as brave and loyal, and this presentation became part of the national story. Bean had been a war correspondent and was involved with the memorial, so his context affected the way he recorded the war. He was a product of his time, and he wanted Australians to remember the war in a particular way.

Bill Gammage’s The Broken Years is different. He used the letters and diaries of soldiers, which allowed him to show the experiences of ordinary men. Gammage wrote in the 1970s, when social history was becoming important, so his interest in ordinary soldiers reflects his own time. This shows that the same war can be recorded in different ways by different historians.

Ken Inglis wrote about war memorials and argued that the Anzac story had become a kind of civil religion. He looked closely at the memorials and ceremonies, which the other historians did not. This supports the statement because his interest in the memorials reflects the questions of his own period.

Lake and Reynolds wrote What’s Wrong with Anzac? when Anzac Day was becoming more popular. They argued that the Anzac story had become too important in Australian history. This is another context that shapes how history is recorded. Their account is a useful counterweight to the earlier accounts, because it shows what the national story left out.

However, the statement is not entirely true. The soldiers’ letters and diaries were real evidence, and historians had to use them. Historians are shaped by their contexts, but they cannot change the evidence.

In conclusion, the recording of history for the Anzacs is shaped by historians’ contexts, but the evidence also limits what they can say.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The case study is Appeasement, and the area of debate is whether Britain’s policy towards Nazi Germany between 1935 and 1939 was a reasonable strategy for buying time or a moral and strategic failure. Mary Beard’s claim that the role of the academic is to make everything less simple concerns the aims and purposes of the producers of history, and I agree with it to a considerable extent. The historiography of appeasement has moved from a simple moral story towards a more complex one. The complication has not been an end in itself, however, and some historians who complicated the story offered single answers of their own.

The orthodox account, given most influentially by Winston Churchill in The Gathering Storm (1948), treated appeasement as a failure of nerve by men who should have confronted Hitler earlier. It turned the period into a moral contrast between appeasers and resisters, and it made Munich, agreed on 30 September 1938, the decisive act of folly. The orthodoxy was not wrong about every fact, but it judged the choices of 1935 to 1939 by what was known later, and the decision-makers did not have that knowledge.

The complication begins with the record itself. Chamberlain’s statement on his return from Munich, ‘peace for our time’, was read by contemporaries as a promise, but British rearmament in 1938 was not ready for a major war, and the Anglo-German Naval Agreement of 1935 had reflected a wish to limit German power by negotiation. Historians who work from the cabinet papers find men weighing the cost of war against a German victory they could not measure. The same documents can support Churchill’s judgement of folly or a view of a reasonable gamble, which is why the evidence itself produces complication.

A.J.P. Taylor’s The Origins of the Second World War (1961) complicated the orthodoxy in the way Source C predicts. Taylor argued that Hitler behaved like a traditional German statesman, seeking revision of the Versailles settlement through opportunist diplomacy rather than following a fixed plan of conquest, and that the British and French had reasonable grounds to think him satisfiable. The book was controversial, and critics said Taylor gave too little weight to Hitler’s ideology. Its complication was nonetheless a real gain for the field, because it forced historians to ask what Hitler wanted and what London and Paris believed he wanted.

Gerhard Weinberg complicated Taylor in turn. In The Foreign Policy of Hitler’s Germany (1970), based on German, British and American archives, he argued that Hitler’s diplomacy followed an ideological programme, including the aim of expansion in the east, and that the moves of 1933 to 1936 were steps in that programme rather than improvised opportunism. The argument restored Hitler’s intentions to the centre of the story. Weinberg shows the reader that one interpretation of Hitler’s aims has been replaced by another, and that the choice between them depends on which archive is trusted.

Donald Cameron Watt’s How War Came (1989) complicated the picture again. Watt used newly opened archives to show how British and French diplomats misread Hitler’s intentions, and how misperceptions and misleading advice shaped decisions as the clock ticked towards war. He argued that Hitler’s own drive for war in 1939 had to be weighed against the choices made at Munich, rather than treated as a simple result of appeasement. Watt’s account rejects the familiar caricature of appeasers and anti-appeasers, and it presents the policy as a problem of information as well as of morality.

Yet the statement has limits. Complication is not always the academic’s purpose, and some historians simplified while complicating. Taylor’s thesis that Hitler was an opportunist was a bold claim that many readers took as a new orthodoxy, and Weinberg’s programme thesis replaced one clear story with another. When historians present complexity as the final answer they risk a relativism in which no account can be preferred to another. The academic’s real role is to test interpretations against evidence and to show which complications matter. Beard’s claim is most useful when read as a claim about method rather than a claim that every position is equally complicated.

I agree to a considerable extent that the academic’s role is to make everything less simple. The appeasement debate shows that the orthodox story was simplified by its authors and that later historians complicated it with new evidence, new accounts of intention and new studies of misperception. Taylor, Weinberg and Watt each made the story harder to tell and gave the reader a more defined question to answer. The academic also simplifies in another sense, by reducing a mass of evidence to a thesis, and the best historians of appeasement have done both.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 21–25 row: it names the case study and the area of debate at the start, gives a judgement on Source C that is sustained across the debate, and treats Taylor, Weinberg and Watt as competing positions that each add complication.

The case study I have chosen is Appeasement. The area of debate is whether appeasement was a reasonable policy or a failure. Source C says that the role of the academic is to make everything less simple. I think this is partly true, because historians of appeasement have made the picture more complicated, but I do not fully agree.

Churchill is an important figure in the story of appeasement. In The Gathering Storm he presented the appeasers as weak men who let Hitler grow stronger. This version was simple and had a clear moral lesson. Later historians disagreed with it and offered a more complex picture. They looked at the documents and found that the British government had reasons for its choices, including the state of its armed forces and the fear of another war.

A.J.P. Taylor is one historian who complicated the story. In The Origins of the Second World War he argued that Hitler was not a planned conqueror but an opportunist. This made historians think about what Hitler actually wanted. Other historians, such as Gerhard Weinberg, disagreed and argued that Hitler had a clear plan. The debate shows that the academic makes things less simple because each historian adds something that makes the earlier account harder to accept.

However, I do not think the academic always makes things less simple. Some historians present their own single answer, and this can make the story simpler again. Taylor’s opportunist thesis was itself a simple explanation that many readers accepted. So while Source C describes an important part of historical work, the academic also has to reduce evidence to an argument.

In conclusion, I partly agree with Source C. The debate about appeasement has become more complex, and historians have shown that the choices of the 1930s were difficult. But complexity is not the only goal of history, and historians also make simpler arguments that can be tested. Historians who make the story harder to tell are doing necessary work, but the reader still has to decide which complication matters most.

sampleAnswers.answer:
My case study is Athenian democracy, from the reforms of Cleisthenes in 508/7 BC to its suppression in the late fourth century BC. One of the areas of debate I examine is how far ordinary citizens, rather than elites, shaped Athenian decisions. The statement in Source B is that historians are able to reach truth from their analysis. Applied to the methods of historians in this debate, the statement holds to a considerable extent for the methods that test individual facts. It holds much less for the methods that reconstruct the political life of the citizen body, where historians reach competing but defensible accounts rather than one truth.

The methods of historians that most support the statement are source criticism and corroboration. Historians ask who produced a source, for what purpose, and whether other evidence confirms it. Athenian inscriptions and ostraka, the potsherds on which citizens scratched the names of men they wished to exile, can be checked against literary references and placed in their archaeological context. This kind of evidence lets historians establish particular facts with confidence, such as how the procedure of ostracism worked. In this sense analysis does produce reliable knowledge about the institutions of democracy.

The debate becomes harder once the evidence concerns the power of citizens. No full attendance records survive, so participation has to be inferred from procedures, from the rhetoric addressed to audiences, and from institutions that needed large numbers of citizens to act. Josiah Ober, in Mass and Elite in Democratic Athens (1989), argues that ordinary citizens exercised real political power through the Assembly and the law courts, and that elites depended on the consent of the citizen body. His case is strongest in the courts, where juries of several hundred citizens were chosen by lot. Ober reads the rhetoric of the orators alongside the institutions, treating the speeches as evidence of what politicians needed to say to win the citizen body's support. M. I. Finley's Democracy Ancient and Modern (1973) stressed the dependence of Athenian democracy on slavery and the exclusion of women and resident foreigners from citizenship. Those who emphasise these limits read the same institutions as evidence of a narrower political community. The two readings differ because they begin from different questions, not because one has misread the sources, so analysis yields defensible interpretations rather than a single truth.

A further problem sits behind both readings. Thucydides states that the speeches in his history were reconstructed to convey the general sense of what was said, so the Funeral Oration attributed to Pericles is at least partly his own account of Athenian democracy. The Constitution of the Athenians, attributed to Aristotle, and the pamphlet of an anonymous oligarch hostile to democracy were also shaped by their authors' purposes. The citizen body itself was defined by law: Pericles' citizenship law of 451/450 BC restricted citizenship to those with two Athenian parents, so the category historians count depends on definitions the sources supply. Historians therefore analyse these texts as interpretations, and the analysis reaches the most probable reading of what Athenians believed.

Overall, the statement applies to a considerable extent to the methods that verify facts, which allow historians to establish a reliable account of how the institutions worked. It applies much less to the question of whose voice shaped Athenian democracy, because the sources are few, mostly written by elites or for persuasion, and the debate turns on interpretive models as much as on evidence. Historians reach the best-supported account rather than truth in full, and the historiography of Athenian democracy shows that competing analyses of the same evidence can each be defensible.

My case study is Athenian democracy. The area of debate is whether ordinary Athenians had real power, or whether a small group of wealthy and educated men controlled the democracy. Source B says historians can reach truth from their analysis. Historians do use their sources to find out what happened, but the sources for Athens are limited and were written by people who had their own opinions.

Historians use methods such as checking sources against each other. Inscriptions and ostraka can confirm that certain events happened, such as the ostracism of politicians. Decrees that were inscribed on stone can be compared with what the literary sources say about the Assembly and the courts, and historians look at when and why an author was writing. These methods show that analysis can produce reliable information about how the Assembly and courts worked, so the statement is partly true.

However, the sources are a problem. Thucydides put speeches into the mouths of his speakers, including Pericles, and he admits they are not word for word. The Constitution of the Athenians may have been written by a student of Aristotle rather than by Aristotle himself. An oligarch also wrote against the democracy. Because most of the sources come from elites, historians have to be careful about what they claim about ordinary people.

Josiah Ober argues that ordinary citizens had a lot of influence through the Assembly and the law courts. Others stress the exclusion of women, slaves and foreigners from the citizen body. Those who doubt Ober's view point out that individual leaders often proposed the decrees the Assembly passed, so the evidence can be read as elite direction. Both sides rely on the same speeches and decrees, which is why the debate turns on interpretation as much as on evidence. This debate shows that historians can disagree even when using the same sources, so analysis does not always give one truth.

Overall the statement applies in some ways but not others. Historians can establish facts about the democracy, but it is harder to say how much ordinary people shaped decisions.

sampleAnswers.answer:
My case study is the Crusades, and the area of debate is the motivation of the crusaders: why men took the cross, and what they hoped to gain. Historians have answered this question in different ways because they have used different kinds of evidence. The changing methods of historians do not simply add new facts. They change what counts as evidence for a motive, and so they change the answer. This response argues that the shifts from chronicle narrative to papal documents, from documents to the records of individual crusaders, and from Latin sources to the sources of the Muslim world have each reshaped the debate, but that each method has also produced its own limits.

The older narrative histories relied on the chronicles written by the crusaders and their clerics, and their method was to tell the story of the expeditions in sequence. Joseph François Michaud's Histoire des croisades (1812–1822) presented the Crusades as an epic of faith and adventure. Steven Runciman's A History of the Crusades (1951–1954) built a more critical narrative from the same kinds of chronicle, but it still read motive from the character of the leaders. In this method the crusaders were pious, greedy or restless according to what the chronicles chose to show, and the question of motive was answered through the personalities of a few leaders.

Carl Erdmann's Die Entstehung des Kreuzzugsgedankens (1935) changed the method. Erdmann used papal letters, councils and sermons to ask when and how the idea of a crusade took shape. His evidence was ideological rather than narrative: it showed the Church constructing a concept of holy war with its own purposes. Because the question shifted from what leaders intended to how an idea was formed, motive became a matter of ecclesiastical ideas and papal policy. This source criticism moved the debate away from character and towards the institutions that gave the expeditions their meaning.

Jonathan Riley-Smith's work from the 1970s and 1980s changed the method again. In What Were the Crusades? (1977) and The First Crusade and the Idea of Crusading (1986), he argued that the crusaders were motivated chiefly by spiritual concerns, especially penance and the remission of sins, and that the crusade was a form of pilgrimage. To test this, he used the charters, wills and family records that individual crusaders left behind. The method made motive measurable. A family's gifts to churches before departure could be read as evidence of penitential intent. Earlier narratives had assumed motives, and this approach tested them against the records.

Later historians have criticised the spiritual model, and their methods have widened the sources. Christopher Tyerman's God's War: A New History of the Crusades (2006) stresses mixed motives, including politics, land, kinship and the pressures of lordship, and warns against reducing the expeditions to a single explanation. Carole Hillenbrand's The Crusades: Islamic Perspectives (1999) brings Arabic sources into the historiography. Those sources show that the crusaders were one party in a wider conflict, and that the motives of Muslim rulers and communities shaped events as much as the motives of the crusaders. Amin Maalouf's The Crusades Through Arab Eyes made the same point for a general readership. The debate is now about whose motives count, not only which motives are the true ones.

Edward Said's Orientalism (1978) gave historians a further method: to examine how Western writers constructed the East and their own identity against it. Applied to the Crusades, the approach asks whether the category of crusade was itself a later construction. Erdmann and Riley-Smith both suggested that the idea developed over time rather than appearing fully formed. If the idea is a construction, the motive of the crusaders must be read as part of a changing ideology, not as a fixed fact. This method is therefore less a source of new answers than a challenge to the question itself.

The changing methods of historians have reshaped the debate about crusaders' motives in several steps: from narrative character to documentary idea, from documentary idea to measurable personal intention, and from Latin intention to a multi-sided conflict. Each step has been driven by a new kind of source, and each has produced new limits. Chronicles favour the leaders who commissioned them, charters favour landholding families, and Arabic chronicles were written for purposes of their own. The method shapes the answer because it decides which motives can be seen at all. Historians have not converged on a final explanation for why men took the cross, but the methods have made the question sharper. They have forced historians to say which evidence supports which motive, and whose motives the sources record. Changing methods have shaped the interpretations substantially, but mainly by widening the set of voices that must be heard.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The Crusades offer a clear case of changing methods reshaping an area of debate: why men took the cross. Early narrative histories relied on the chronicles, and Steven Runciman's A History of the Crusades (1951–1954) built a critical narrative from them. Motive in that work was read from the character of the leaders, so the crusaders appeared pious or greedy according to the writer's view. The method limited the answer to what the chronicles chose to record, and it said little about the ideas behind the expeditions.

Carl Erdmann's Die Entstehung des Kreuzzugsgedankens (1935) changed the method by using papal letters and sermons to trace how the idea of a crusade developed. Erdmann asked when and how the idea took shape, rather than what the leaders intended. This moved motive from individual character to the ideas of the Church, and so the answer to why men took the cross became a question about ideology.

Jonathan Riley-Smith went further in What Were the Crusades? (1977). He used the charters, wills and family records of crusaders to argue that spiritual motives, especially penance, were central. The method made motive a question about evidence that could be tested in documents. Riley-Smith's approach shows how a change in the type of source changes the answer the historian can give, because the records he used could confirm or contradict the claims made by the chronicles.

More recent historians have criticised these models for relying on Western sources. Carole Hillenbrand's The Crusades: Islamic Perspectives (1999) uses Arabic sources and shows that the Crusades were one part of a wider conflict. This reshapes the debate, because it is no longer only about the crusaders' motives but also about the interests of the people they met. Changing methods have therefore widened the debate rather than closing it, although each new source also brings its own limits. A student who compares Erdmann with Riley-Smith sees that the question of motive changes with the documents chosen, and that the change is not a simple advance. The best answers therefore explain which sources they trust and why, rather than treating the newest method as the final word.

Historians today debate whether the crusaders were motivated mainly by religion or by land and power, and the methods they use help decide which answer they reach. sampleAnswers.answer:
Historical evidence shapes the construction of history to a considerable extent, but it sets the limits of an account rather than dictating its final form. Norman Wilson and Giselle Byrnes describe two levels at which evidence works. For Wilson, evidence is the force that revises a historian's argument from within the process of research. For Byrnes, the surviving record decides which stories can be told at all, and the questions that give the record its meaning come from the present. This response argues that evidence determines what can be said about the past, while the historian's questions and selections determine what is built from it.

Wilson's account gives evidence real power. Historians begin with a problem and a hypothesis, but they look for evidence, and that evidence 'will not always fit' the original hypothesis. The historian therefore modifies the argument, and the result is a process in which evidence and hypothesis 'constantly modify each other'. Wilson concludes that historians never seem to write the book they set out to write, which is a direct demonstration of evidence shaping construction. Yet the same passage shows that the historian is not a passive reader. Historians 'tend to discard evidence' that seems irrelevant to their purposes, so the record is trimmed by the purposes the historian brings to it. This selection of evidence is an act of the historian, not of the record.

Byrnes locates a second limit in the surviving record. Historians 'can only work with those pieces that remain', and because the past cannot be recreated in its totality, every history begins from fragments. Her point about silence is more telling. Her observation that 'some stories are told' while 'others are silenced' means that the absence of evidence is itself a shaping force. A community that kept no archive cannot be written about with the same confidence as one that did, and the shape of the surviving record shapes the history that follows. Evidence therefore constructs history by its absence as well as by what historians do with it.

Byrnes, however, denies that evidence determines the questions. She argues that the questions put to the past are 'invariably shaped by our present', and she notes that most historians no longer believe in a gold standard of objectivity. The quest for objectivity is, in her phrase, 'like nailing jelly to the wall'. If the evidence were the decisive force, two historians with the same records would produce the same history. They do not, because the present determines which questions make the evidence relevant. This is also why Wilson's historians discard material: the purposes that decide relevance come from outside the archive, from the historian's own time. The historiography of objectivity has long turned on this point.

A third source makes the case from another direction. E. H. Carr's What is History? (1961) argues that facts do not speak for themselves and that the historian decides which facts to use and in what context. On this view evidence is inert until the historian gives it a place in an argument. Thucydides shows the same problem in the ancient world, and his historical method makes it visible. Where he could not recall the exact words of speeches, he composed them himself and openly admitted that he had done so, so the gaps in his evidence were filled by judgement that shaped the history he wrote. Ranke's ideal that history should show the past 'as it actually happened' expresses the opposite aspiration, an account governed entirely by evidence. Thucydides and Carr show why that ideal is difficult to reach.

The sources therefore agree on the limits of evidence and disagree about where the rest of history comes from. Wilson places the decisive force in the dialogue between evidence and argument, Byrnes places it in the present that asks the questions, and Carr places it in the historian's choices. A sustained evaluation shows that evidence is necessary, because history cannot be written without it and the record defines its boundaries. It is not sufficient, because the same evidence can support different histories when different questions and purposes are brought to it. Evidence shapes construction to a considerable extent, but the historian's judgement completes the shaping.

The historian who wishes to explain the role of evidence must therefore analyse both the record and the purposes that give it meaning. Evidence is the foundation of history and the most constraining influence on it, yet history is constructed through questions, selection and argument, and these come from the present as much as from the past. How far evidence shapes history depends on how far historians allow it to qualify their purposes. Wilson's account suggests that the best historians do allow this, even when it forces them to abandon the book they intended.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: it argues a sustained judgement that evidence constrains history while the historian's questions and selection construct it, and it integrates Sources A and B and Carr and Thucydides throughout. sampleAnswers.answer:
Historical evidence has a large effect on the construction of history, though not the whole effect. Norman Wilson argues that historians begin with a hypothesis and then look for evidence, and that the evidence often does not fit, so the historian revises the argument. Historians also discard evidence that seems irrelevant to them. This shows that evidence constrains the argument, but also that the historian chooses what to keep, so the record is selected as well as read.

Giselle Byrnes makes a different point. She says that we can only work with the pieces of the past that remain, and that some stories are told while others are silenced. Evidence that survives shapes what history can say, because a community that left no records cannot be written about in the same way as one that did. Byrnes also argues that the questions we ask are shaped by our present values, so the evidence is always read through the present. The same records can therefore produce different histories in different periods.

E. H. Carr's What is History? (1961) supports this view. Carr argued that facts do not speak for themselves and that historians choose which facts to use. Evidence on its own does not produce history, and the historian's judgement is needed to give it a place in an argument. Thucydides also shows the limits of evidence. Where he could not recall the exact words of speeches, he wrote speeches that he judged the speakers would have given, so evidence ran out and judgement took its place. His candour about this makes the method easier to judge.

Overall, evidence shapes the construction of history to a considerable extent because it sets limits on what historians can write. The question is therefore one of degree, and the sources help to measure it. Wilson's historians select, Byrnes's historians ask questions from the present, and Carr's historians choose facts. Carr's point also applies to the sources themselves, since Wilson and Byrnes choose their examples as well. Evidence is therefore important, but it does not determine the history on its own.

Byrnes says that historians only have the pieces of the past that remain, and that the past is always seen through the present. Both sources show that evidence matters for history. Carr also said that facts do not speak for themselves and that historians choose them. So evidence is important, but historians also decide what it means. This is why different historians can write different histories about the same events, and why the view of history changes over time.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The case study is Napoleon Bonaparte, and the area of historical debate is whether Napoleon consolidated the gains of the French Revolution or betrayed them. Forms of historical communication have shaped how that question has been answered, so the form has done more than carry an interpretation: it has helped to produce it. Three forms matter most here: the memoir that gave Napoleon’s own account of his career, the painted and official images that made him heroic, and the scholarly biography that tested the legend against the archive. Each selected, framed and simplified what readers came to believe, and so each shaped the historical interpretations that followed.

Emmanuel de Las Cases published Le Mémorial de Sainte-Hélène in 1823, two years after Napoleon died on Saint Helena. Its written form, a day-by-day journal of conversations with the exiled emperor, gave readers the sense of hearing Napoleon directly. The Mémorial fed the legend that grew after 1815, in which Napoleon carried the principles of the Revolution across Europe and was then betrayed by his enemies. Historians must treat it as a source with a purpose, because Las Cases recorded and shaped Napoleon’s reflections for readers who were often critical of the restored Bourbon monarchy. The intimate, conversational form made the legend look like testimony rather than argument, and that appearance helped it last.

The visual and official forms of war shaped the same legend in another register. Jacques-Louis David’s heroic images of Bonaparte crossing the Alps presented the general as a figure of will and destiny, not as a commander whose army depended on supplies and artillery. Napoleon’s own Bulletins of the Grande Armée were official communication designed to sustain support at home, and their reports of victory must be read as propaganda rather than neutral accounts. These forms did not record events. They created the Napoleon that later writers had to explain, including the idea that his victories were the product of personal genius.

Leo Tolstoy’s War and Peace, published in parts between 1865 and 1869, is a novel, and its form made it an argument about history. In the epilogue Tolstoy rejected the view that the will of one man caused the invasion of Russia, and argued that the movements of many people were the real forces behind events. The novel followed ordinary soldiers and aristocrats through the campaign, so readers saw Napoleon from the outside, small in the face of events. This form shaped a long debate about whether great individuals or structural forces make history. The novel did not prove Tolstoy’s theory, but it made the theory persuasive to readers who would never open a historical treatise.

Scholarly biography added a third form and a different interpretation. Georges Lefebvre’s Napoléon treated Napoleon in relation to the social and political changes of the Revolution, and read the Civil Code and the centralised administration as partly continuing revolutionary reform. This approach moved attention from Napoleon’s will to the record of institutions and society. Military historians such as David Chandler, whose The Campaigns of Napoleon (1966) reconstructs the campaigns in detail, moved attention again, to logistics, orders and the conditions in which decisions were made. Each form selected different evidence, and each selection implied a different Napoleon.

The debate between heir and betrayer is therefore shaped by form. A memoir invites a reading of Napoleon as a victim of enemies, a painting invites a reading of him as heroic will, a scholarly biography ties him to the social record, and a novel makes him a test of whether individuals matter at all. Andrew Roberts’s Napoleon: A Life (2014) brings scholarly and popular forms together, combining a narrative of the career with detailed use of the archive. A single well-written biography can still give a reader a coherent Napoleon, and that is why interpretation depends on the form in which it reaches the reader.

Form has shaped the interpretation of Napoleon in a sustained way. Las Cases made the legend look like testimony, David made Napoleon’s will the centre of the story, Tolstoy made him a limit on the argument about great men, and scholarly biography tied his career to the record of the Revolution. Interpretation has changed as the forms have changed. Historians who want to judge this debate must first ask who wrote, pictured or narrated Napoleon, for which audience and in what form, because the answer to heir or betrayer has been decided as much by the medium as by the evidence. The question is therefore one of form as well as evidence.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The case study is Napoleon, and the debate I will discuss is whether Napoleon was the heir of the Revolution or its betrayer. The form in which Napoleon was written and pictured has affected how historians answer this question. I will explain four forms that have influenced interpretation.

The first is the memoir. Las Cases published the Mémorial de Sainte-Hélène in 1823. It recorded Napoleon’s conversations on Saint Helena and presented him as a victim of his enemies. Because it was written as a journal of conversations, readers felt they heard Napoleon directly. This form helped create the legend that Napoleon had spread the ideas of the Revolution and been betrayed. Historians have had to treat the Mémorial carefully because it was written for a particular audience.

The second form is the painting. David’s images of Napoleon crossing the Alps show him as a heroic figure. Images like this gave the public an idea of Napoleon as a man of will. Official communication such as the Bulletins also described his victories in a favourable way. These forms shaped how Napoleon was understood, so interpretation was affected by what was shown and reported.

The third form is the scholarly biography. Lefebvre’s study connected Napoleon to the Revolution and the Civil Code. This gives a different view, because it makes Napoleon part of the history of institutions rather than a single person. Chandler’s study of the campaigns is also useful because it looks at military decisions in detail.

Tolstoy’s novel War and Peace is a fourth form, and it argued that great individuals did not cause events in the way people thought. This made readers question whether Napoleon was important, and it contributed to the debate about great men.

Form and interpretation are linked. Each form selects some things and leaves others out, so the historian has to consider how the source was produced. The debate about heir or betrayer has therefore been shaped by the forms through which Napoleon reached readers. A reader who understands this can ask of any account what it leaves out, and why that omission suited the person who wrote it.

sampleAnswers.answer:
My case study is Elizabeth I of England, and the two areas of debate are the nature of the religious settlement and the construction of her public image. Gaddis argues in Source C that historians stand on 'squishy ground', and that there is 'little basis for claiming any consensus at all' about what the past might tell us. The question asks whether historical debate informs our understanding of the past. This response argues that debate informs understanding to a considerable extent, because it reveals the assumptions and sources on which each reading of Elizabeth rests. But the debates also show that Gaddis is partly right. On the two questions examined here, no consensus has emerged, so understanding is provisional rather than settled.

The first debate concerns the religious settlement of 1559. Older accounts presented Elizabeth as a Protestant queen who completed the English Reformation. Christopher Haigh's English Reformations (1993) challenged this view by arguing that the Reformation was imposed from above, and that many parishes remained attached to the old rites well into her reign. Eamon Duffy's The Stripping of the Altars (1992) had earlier insisted that traditional religion was deeply rooted and popular before the break. Patrick Collinson's The Elizabethan Puritan Movement (1967) added a third pressure, showing that the godly wanted a more thorough reform than the queen was prepared to grant. Each reading draws on different evidence: Haigh on local records and church court business, Duffy on the material culture of parishes, and Collinson on the writings of the Puritans.

The second debate concerns Elizabeth's public image. Frances Yates's Astraea: The Imperial Theme in the Sixteenth Century (1975) read the cult of the virgin queen as a deliberate imperial myth, drawing on classical and Renaissance symbolism. Roy Strong's Gloriana: The Portraits of Queen Elizabeth I (1987) studied the portraits and processions through which the image was disseminated, and argued that it was carefully controlled. Carole Levin's The Heart and Stomach of a King (1994) changed the emphasis by asking how gender shaped the politics of the queen's rule and how she used her position. The evidence here is visual and ceremonial, and the interpretation depends on whether the image is read as propaganda or as a constraint the queen had to manage.

Debate has informed understanding in three ways. First, it has exposed the assumption of the older narratives that a Protestant or national identity could be read straight from the sources. Haigh and Duffy show that the same parish evidence can support opposite conclusions, depending on what the historian expects to find. Second, it has shown that the image of Elizabeth was produced rather than simply observed, as Yates and Strong demonstrate. Third, it has moved the question from the queen's personality to the institutions and audiences that gave her power its meaning. Each of these is a real gain in understanding, because each identifies what an account of Elizabeth must explain.

Gaddis is nonetheless right that consensus has not been reached. Haigh and Duffy disagree about how far the people of England wanted reform, and further evidence has not resolved that disagreement. Historians who study the image disagree about whether the queen was a shrewd manager of appearances or a ruler whose gender forced her to adopt a constructed persona. Each side can point to the same portraits and speeches. Gaddis's image of squishy ground captures the problem: the debate exposes the evidence but does not settle its meaning. Where a consensus is missing, historians must be explicit about the assumptions behind each conclusion.

The debate nevertheless informs understanding in a second sense. Even without consensus, the disputes show what each reading of Elizabeth depends on: an account of faith, an account of power, or an account of gender. A student who reads Haigh and Duffy learns that a reformation can be measured by the survival of practice as well as by the legal settlement. A student who reads Yates and Strong learns that power in the sixteenth century was exercised through images. These are understandings that a single narrative would not provide. The understanding is provisional, but it is real, because it identifies which questions can be answered and which remain open.

Historical debate informs our understanding of the past to a considerable extent, because it exposes the assumptions, sources and questions behind any account of Elizabeth I. Gaddis is right that consensus is absent on the religious settlement and on the image of the queen, and the debates show that understanding is provisional. Yet a provisional understanding is still an understanding. The debates over Elizabeth show that the past can be known through its contested readings, even when the contest is never settled. Debate does not tell us what happened with certainty, but it tells us what we must explain and why historians have explained it differently. The historiography of the period is therefore a map of the questions, not a set of final answers.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: it names Elizabeth I and two areas of debate, sets historians against each other on each, and tests Gaddis's claim about consensus against what debate actually reveals. The conclusion makes a judgement that understanding is provisional but real.

sampleAnswers.answer:
My response examines two areas of debate about Elizabeth I: the nature of the religious settlement and the construction of her public image. Gaddis is right that there is little consensus in these debates, but the debates still tell us something about the past, and the question is how much.

Christopher Haigh's English Reformations (1993) argues that the Reformation was imposed from above and that many parishes remained attached to the old rites. Eamon Duffy's The Stripping of the Altars (1992) argues that traditional religion was popular and deeply rooted. The two historians disagree about how far people wanted reform, and they use the same kind of parish evidence to reach different conclusions. This disagreement shows that understanding depends on what the historian expects to find, and that a single source type can support opposite readings.

Frances Yates's Astraea (1975) reads the cult of the virgin queen as a deliberate imperial myth, while Roy Strong's Gloriana (1987) studies the portraits and processions through which the image was controlled. Carole Levin's The Heart and Stomach of a King (1994) asks how gender shaped the queen's rule. These historians show that Elizabeth's image was produced, and that the production of images was part of her politics, although they differ on how deliberate that production was.

Gaddis claims that historians stand on squishy ground, but the debates show that the ground can be mapped. They do not produce a consensus, yet they show what each reading assumes, and that is a real gain in understanding. Gaddis's claim is strongest where the sources are most open to opposed readings, and the Elizabethan settlement is a clear example. The debate about Haigh and Duffy does not show that historians know less about the period than before. It shows that the questions have become sharper, and that the evidence now has to be weighed against assumptions that were once invisible. Historical debate therefore informs our understanding of Elizabeth I to a considerable extent, although the understanding remains provisional and the areas of debate remain open. A good answer also says which reading is more persuasive, and why, rather than leaving the reader with a list of views.
