sampleAnswers.answer: Elizabeth I was a Protestant queen and historians have debated her religion. Some historians think the Reformation was imposed and others think it was popular. Elizabeth's image was also important, and historians like Yates and Strong have written about her portraits. Gaddis says historians do not agree, which is true for these debates. So historical debate shows there are different views about Elizabeth and her reign, and this helps us understand the past in some way. The debates are about different kinds of evidence, which is one reason they have not been settled.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Historiographical debate has changed approaches to the construction of history over time, most of all by making the constructed nature of narrative visible to historians and readers. The debate over counterfactual history shows this in an unusually sharp form. Niall Ferguson argues that counterfactuals restore the uncertainty of people who did not yet know how events would turn out, and Mads Mordhorst argues that counterfactual history is itself a narrative built from choices. Their disagreement is a debate about whether any history can escape narrative determinism. The debate has changed how historians think and write, but it has not produced a method free of the problems it exposes.

The debate has changed approaches by making narrative choice a subject of argument. E.H. Carr’s What Is History? (1961) had already argued that facts become history only through the historian’s selection and interpretation, and Hayden White’s Metahistory (1973) argued that historical works are shaped by literary structures of plot and argument. Once these claims were accepted, a chronological account could no longer be treated as a neutral reflection of the past. Ferguson’s Source A is a product of that change. He says historians should be alive to the counterfactual and try to recapture the uncertainty of contemporaries, because ‘there are forks in the road’. The argument presents the past as open rather than as a path that is ‘somehow predestined’. Counterfactual history therefore takes the method of narrative and makes it explicit.

Mordhorst’s Source B argues that this approach has not escaped the problem it criticises. He points out that counterfactual history rests on the belief that a real history exists, and that the counterfactual narrative must be counter to a factual one. Ferguson admits that the form of historical narrative has created what he calls ‘narrative determinism’, but Mordhorst argues that Ferguson has the problem upside down. The problem is not isolated to traditional history, because counterfactual history is also a constructed narrative and carries the same difficulties. Mordhorst’s point is that the debate has revealed the problem without solving it.

The debate has shaped the construction of history in two ways. It has encouraged historians to write openly about contingency, setting out the options open to people at the time, and to test whether determinism lies in the sources or in the narrative. It has also made historians more cautious about claims to objectivity. Richard Evans, in In Defence of History (1997), defended the historical profession against relativist critics and argued that constructed narratives can still be tested against evidence. Evans’s position answers Mordhorst’s worry in part. Counterfactual narratives are constructions, but their premises can be checked against sources, and a constructed narrative is not for that reason as valid as any other.

The debate has also changed how historians reach the public. Source A is an interview published as a podcast, and its form makes the argument conversational. Ferguson speaks in a way a reader of a monograph would not expect, and the listener hears the historian reflect on his own method. This is a change in construction: the account of how the historian works becomes part of the historical argument, and the audience can judge the method as well as the conclusion. The approach carries risk, because a spoken argument can be persuasive without being checked, but it shows that historiographical debate now travels through forms that did not exist when Carr wrote.

The debate’s influence has limits, however. Counterfactual history remains a minority method, and most historians still write chronological narratives. Ferguson’s appeal to contemporaries’ uncertainty is powerful, but it depends on the same sources that Mordhorst says are already structured by narrative. A historian who writes ‘what if’ still chooses which alternatives count as real, so the counterfactual does not remove the choice. It makes the choice visible. The debate has therefore changed how narrative is constructed, but not the fact that construction is required.

Historiographical debate has changed approaches to the construction of history considerably, but in a bounded way. It has made narrative a subject of explicit argument, given historians a method for showing contingency, and forced them to test assumptions about determinism. Ferguson and Mordhorst show, however, that the debate has not produced a history without narrative. Its clearest effect is that historians now state their choices rather than hide them, and the choices themselves have become part of the historiography. The debate has also made historians more aware of their readers, who can now see the alternatives and judge the narrative against them.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Historiographical debate has changed approaches to the construction of history, and Sources A and B show two sides of this. Source A is Niall Ferguson’s defence of counterfactual history, and Source B is Mads Mordhorst’s criticism of it. Both sources are about how history is constructed, so the debate is useful for evaluating how history is made.

Ferguson argues that counterfactual history is valuable because it shows the choices people faced at the time. He says there are ‘forks in the road’, and that historians who see only the path that was taken write as if events were predetermined. This is an argument against determinism, and it suggests that the debate has changed history by making historians consider alternatives. Ferguson also says that historians should try to recapture the uncertainty that contemporaries felt. This is important because it asks historians to explain their choices.

Mordhorst argues that counterfactual history is not free of the problems it criticises. He says it is built on the idea of a real history, and that it is still a narrative. He claims Ferguson has the problem upside down, because the same narrative problems apply to counterfactual history. This suggests the debate has shown that all history is constructed.

Other historians matter here too. E.H. Carr’s What Is History? argued that historians select and interpret facts, so the construction of history depends on the historian. This supports the view that debate has changed how historians see their work. Hayden White’s work on narrative structure also contributes, because it suggests that historical works use the forms of plot.

Richard Evans, in In Defence of History, also matters, because he argues that constructed narratives can still be tested against evidence. That claim answers Mordhorst in part, since a counterfactual narrative can be checked against its premises even if it remains a construction. The debate has changed approaches to history, but not completely. Counterfactual history is still not common, and most historians still write narratives in the traditional way. Its effect is most visible in how historians explain their methods. So the role of historiographical debate is significant but limited.

sampleAnswers.answer: Historians have debated counterfactual history. These sources show that historians argue about how history should be written, and that the debate affects how history is constructed. Carr and other historians also wrote about this. So debate has changed things, but there are still different views about the best method, and the debate has had some effect.

prompts.question: To what extent has changing technology influenced approaches to history over time? Integrate Sources A and B and at least ONE other source throughout your argument.
markerNotes: The strongest answers give a judgement on the extent of technology’s influence: it changes the means of making history, the speed and visibility of revision and the audiences, but it leaves the older questions of authority and selection in place.

Sources A and B must do argumentative work. Foster’s gatekeeping concern and Hughes-Warrington’s point that revision is unevenly distributed should each be tested against the claim, not summarised in turn.

The top answer needs at least one other relevant source, named and explained, for example Elizabeth Eisenstein’s study of print or Roy Rosenzweig and Dan Cohen’s guide to digital history, placed where it supports or complicates the judgement.

Historiographical depth comes from asking whether technology changes the historian’s method or only the public’s access to history, and from testing whether digital revision is more visible than print revision.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Changing technology has influenced approaches to history to a considerable degree, though its greatest effect has been on the means by which history is made, the speed at which it is revised, and the range of people who take part in making it. It has not removed the older questions of authority and selection that have always shaped historical work. Meg Foster’s account of Web 2.0 and Marnie Hughes-Warrington’s account of revision together show that technology changes how the past is produced and corrected, while judgements about whose voice counts remain as contested as before.

The clearest influence is on the production of history. Elizabeth Eisenstein argued that print changed scholarship by making texts fixed and comparable, so that scholars could check one account against another and build on each other’s work. New technologies have extended that change. Roy Rosenzweig and Dan Cohen’s guide Digital History showed how digitised archives, databases and websites let historians gather and present the past in forms a printed monograph could not. Foster’s Source A describes the same shift from the standpoint of public history. Digital platforms have facilitated a greater degree of ‘user engagement’, so the production of history now includes family historians, community groups and museums alongside professional authors. The method has changed as much as the audience. Sources are found through search rather than in the reading room, and the historian must judge the reliability of a website as carefully as a letter.

Technology has also changed the speed and visibility of revision. Hughes-Warrington argues that history is always subject to change, through new editions, corrections and the withdrawal of works from circulation. Digital platforms multiply those changes and make some of them harder to see. In her terms, websites are ‘cached’, hidden rather than deleted. A reader of a printed book could compare the first and second editions on a shelf, while a web page may be altered without a visible trace. Hughes-Warrington also observes that ‘particular kinds of changes catch our eye’, and online attention is uneven in the same way. Technology does not make revision more common across all topics. It makes some revisions, usually those that provoke public controversy, far more visible than the quieter corrections that matter as much to scholars.

The deeper question is authority. Foster warns that the internet raises questions about gatekeeping, authority and the right to speak for the past. Print culture had visible gatekeepers in publishers, editors, referees and appointment committees. Technology lowers the cost of publication so sharply that these gates no longer hold the whole field, but it does not abolish them. Search rankings, platform moderation and popularity now decide what a reader meets first, so the gatekeeping has moved rather than vanished. For historians this changes the approach to evidence and credibility. An argument now sits beside unvetted claims on the same screen, and the task of establishing who speaks, for what purpose and on what evidence has become more urgent. Foster’s concern extends a long problem of historiography rather than creating a new one.

Technology has also widened the audience for history. Foster notes that ideas about the past can now span countries, cultures and languages and reach more people than ever before. Audiences shape what historians write and how they write it. A public historian writing for a blog or a museum app must shorten the argument, show the sources and anticipate readers who may know the material better than the author. The web can make ordinary people contributors and critics, so historical knowledge is now tested in public, often within days of publication. The academic who once wrote for a small readership of specialists has changed in form and in purpose.

There are limits to the claim that technology has transformed historical approaches. Eisenstein, and Rosenzweig and Cohen, are concerned with tools, while the core procedures of historical method have stayed the same. The historian still asks who made a source, why, and what it leaves out. Hughes-Warrington’s point that revision is unevenly distributed shows that professional and social factors decide what is revised, however widely the tools are shared. Technology has therefore influenced the methods, audiences and speed of history more than its philosophy. A historian who regards the past as an argument about evidence will find digital tools useful, but will still need the source criticism that predates them.

Changing technology has therefore influenced approaches to history considerably, but in a bounded way. It has multiplied the producers of history, changed the methods by which sources are found and checked, and made revision both faster and more visible. It has not altered the fundamental questions of authority, selection and evidence that historians have always had to answer, and as public history expands it has made those questions more pressing.

Technology has changed approaches to history in several ways, and in my view the changes are significant but not complete. Sources A and B both show that technology affects history, although they focus on different things.

Source A, by Meg Foster, argues that the web has made history more open, because anyone with access can contribute to understandings of the past through blogs, social media and apps. Foster also says this raises problems of gatekeeping and authority. Source A therefore suggests that technology has changed who produces history but has not settled who has the right to speak for the past.

Source B, by Marnie Hughes-Warrington, is about revision. She says history always changes, but that some changes are welcomed and others are not. Digital platforms make changes faster and sometimes less visible, because a website can be altered or cached. Source B supports the idea that technology has influenced approaches to history because it makes revision different in kind. However, the source also says that particular kinds of changes catch our eye, so technology does not make all revision equal.

Another relevant source is Elizabeth Eisenstein’s work on the printing press. She argued that print made texts fixed and comparable, which helped scholars check each other’s work. Digital technology has done something similar in a new form, since historians can now search archives and find sources quickly. This supports the view that technology has influenced approaches to history, but historians still need to check their sources carefully.

Technology has also influenced the audience for history. Foster notes that ideas about the past can reach more people than before and can span countries and languages. Public historians have to write for readers who can respond quickly, which changes the way they present an argument.

In conclusion, changing technology has influenced approaches to history to a large extent. It has changed how history is produced, how it is revised and who reads it. However, the older problems of evidence and authority remain, and technology has not changed them. The influence is therefore significant but limited.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Audience has become a significant force in the production of history, but its significance is uneven. Jorma Kalela presents the historian as a public figure whose task is to refine the accounts that non-academic audiences hold, and to show why popular views are inadequate. Jerome de Groot describes a historical idea that lives in television, fan fiction, museums and advertising at once, so that the consumption of the past cannot be contained. This response argues that audience is highly significant for the purpose, form and reach of history, but that it has far less influence on the evidence and standards that give history its authority.

Kalela's account treats audience as the setting of the historian's work. He describes historians as referees of public history, who open new perspectives for the people they address and invite them to ponder their values. The audience's significance here lies in purpose. Historians are not simply supplying what the public wants. They must highlight inaccuracies in existing knowledge and show which parts of a popular account are inadequate and why. The historian's work, Kalela says, can be encapsulated as refining non-academic accounts of the past. Audience therefore gives the historian a public task, but it does not lower the standard of argument the historian must meet.

De Groot's concept of historiocopia shows how far the audience has spread. He describes one historical idea living on television, in a Twitter account, in fan fiction, in novels and films, in museum exhibits and as a tea towel. The audience for history is therefore no longer a readership that a historian can address directly. It is a dispersed public of consumers of history, who create, reshape and use the past in forms the historian does not control. This matters because historians must decide which forms to write in and must consider how their work will be taken up. The consumption of the past, de Groot says, is a truly profound and complicated thing.

David Lowenthal's The Past Is a Foreign Country (1985) gives a longer account of this relationship. Lowenthal distinguishes history from heritage, the popular use of the past that is shaped by present needs and identities more than by scholarly inquiry. Heritage is produced for audiences who want reassurance, and its selection of the past reflects that demand. This supports Kalela's concern. When the audience's desire for comfort dominates, the past becomes a source of identity rather than an object of argument. It also qualifies de Groot. Multiplying the audiences for history may increase the variety of the past on offer without increasing its historical accuracy.

The audience matters less to the evidence and method that historians use. The archive is the same whether the reader is a professor or a student watching a documentary, and Kalela's historians test claims against sources, not against popularity. Where audience changes production most is in the choice of topics, the language of the text and the form of the work, whether a scholarly book, a documentary or a museum label. These changes are significant, and de Groot's examples move from the scholarly to the commercial to show how far the forms have multiplied. Yet a change of form does not make an inaccurate claim true, and the historian's standard of proof is not set by the audience. This is a familiar point in the historiography of public history.

There is also a tension between audience demand and historical responsibility. Where publishers or producers reward simple stories, the historian's role as referee becomes harder to fulfil. Kalela's account assumes that historians will act in the public interest, but de Groot's account suggests that the public may not seek correction at all. The significance of audience therefore depends on how historians respond to it. They can accommodate it by simplifying their claims, or they can engage it by showing why a simpler story is wrong. The second response is the historian's proper one, but it requires treating the audience as a critic rather than a customer.

Evaluated overall, audience is highly significant for the form, purpose and reach of history. Kalela shows that it gives the historian a public responsibility, and de Groot shows how widely the past now circulates. Yet the audience has less effect on the evidence and the standards of argument that give history its authority, and Lowenthal's account of heritage shows the risk when audience comfort replaces critical inquiry. The most accurate conclusion is that audience changes what historians write and how they write it, but that its significance for historical truth depends on whether historians keep the referee's role. Audience is therefore a powerful force on the shape of history, and a weaker one on its substance.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Audience has a significant effect on the production of history, but mainly on how history is presented and who it reaches. Jorma Kalela argues that historians have a public role. They act as referees of non-academic accounts of the past, and they must highlight inaccuracies in existing knowledge. The audience is therefore the context in which the historian works, but it does not change the standards the historian must meet, and the historian must still show what is wrong with a popular account and why.

Jerome de Groot's idea of historiocopia shows how many forms the audience now uses. A historical idea can live on television, in fan fiction, in museum exhibits and as a tea towel, and it can be consumed in all of them at once. Historians therefore cannot address a single readership, and they must think about how their work will be taken up by people who may never open a scholarly book. De Groot's point makes the audience look larger and more varied than Kalela's account suggests, and this changes what a historian must consider when writing.

David Lowenthal's The Past Is a Foreign Country (1985) supports the concern that audiences shape history. He argues that heritage is produced for audiences who want reassurance, so the past is selected to suit present needs and identities. When audience demand dominates, history can become a comfort rather than an argument. This is a significant risk for the historian who wants to act as a referee, because the audience may welcome the simpler account and resist the correction.

Overall, audience is significant for the form and reach of history, and it is a serious pressure on how the past is presented. Kalela's historians still test claims against sources, and the audience does not change the evidence. The significance of audience therefore depends on whether historians respond to it by simplifying their claims or by showing why the simpler story is wrong, and the second response is the one a historian should choose. A student who reads both extracts closely will see that audience works through the historian's choices rather than through the evidence itself.
